notes:
I've put these notes together from a limited set of reads. I got through Enduring Word (Guzik), the Bible Hub commentary pages for v. 27 and v. 40, a few StudyLight verse pages, Utley's notes on bible.org, Deffinbaugh's series on bible.org and one Bible Odyssey article. I couldn't reach Wesley's Notes directly, and Calvin's commentary cut off before it reached these verses.

**What I didn't find:** no Catholic or Orthodox material (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), no netbible.org notes, nothing from Lutheran or Pentecostal denominational sites, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace treatment of this passage. I also found no real disagreement between denominations on these verses. The differences I did find are between individual commentators, and I've collected them at the end.

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 23:** Guzik points out the order: the servant handed over the gifts first, as a sign Rebekah answered his prayer, and only then asked about her family. He praised God once he heard she was related to Abraham. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

**v. 24:** Got Questions works out that this makes Rebekah a great-niece to Abraham and second cousin to Isaac. https://www.gotquestions.org/Rebekah-in-the-Bible.html
- Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship) notes that Rebekah belongs to the generation after Isaac. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/children-in-the-hebrew-bible/
- In his note on v. 15, Utley says the name Bethuel means "man of God," which may hint at the family's faith. He adds that the line runs through Milcah, Nahor's true wife, rather than his concubine. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-24

**v. 25:** Mary Baxter reads Rebekah's offer as plain, wholehearted hospitality, with no showing off. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/baxter_mary/WitW/WitW06_Rebekah1.cfm

**v. 26:** Clarke sees two separate acts of worship here: bowing the head, and lying face down on the ground. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-26.html
- Barnes says the bowing shows the old servant's deep thankfulness for God's guidance, and his spoken words go with the gesture. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-29.html
- Baxter notes he wasn't embarrassed to worship in front of a girl he had only just met. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/baxter_mary/WitW/WitW06_Rebekah1.cfm
- Bible Hub's study notes say the Hebrew word for "worship" means bowing down in reverence and submission. https://biblehub.com/genesis/24.htm

**v. 27:**
- *Mercy and truth:* Poole says God showed mercy in promising and truth in keeping the promise. He also suggests the pair may simply mean "true mercy." He takes "brethren" to mean close relatives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-27.htm
- The Geneva Study Bible (Reformed) says the servant does not boast in his good fortune (as the wicked do) but acknowledges that God has dealt mercifully. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-27.htm
- Benson (Methodist) praises the servant for thanking God before he even knew how things would turn out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-27.htm
- Wesley's Notes (Methodist), seen via a StudyLight search result, say these relatives were not idolaters, but worshippers of the true God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-24.html
- Bible Hub's study notes link the words "kindness and faithfulness" to the Hebrew *chesed* and *emet*, God's covenant love and reliability (compare Exodus 34:6). https://biblehub.com/study/genesis/24-27.htm
- "I being in the way": see the differences section below.

**v. 28:** Barnes takes "her mother's house" to mean the women's quarters. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-29.html

**vv. 29–30:** One note on Bible Hub suggests Milcah sent for Laban, Rebekah showed him the gifts, and he then hurried out. Matthew Henry says Laban only came out once he had seen the jewellery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-29.htm
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown think the dazzling gifts made him hurry more and his invitation warmer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_024.cfm
- Guzik notes that Bethuel was still alive, yet Laban took the lead. He suggests Laban may already have been known for driving a good bargain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
- Constable records another view: Bethuel may have been too old, or under his wife's control. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html

**v. 31:** Keil & Delitzsch explain that Laban said "blessed of the LORD" because the servant had already used that name for his master's God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-40.htm

**v. 32:** Barnes says Laban is the one doing all this, including unloading the camels. The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary, citing Murphy, notes the steward evidently had a group of servants with him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/genesis-24.html

**v. 33:** Matthew Henry says doing our duty should come before food, as it did for Jesus (John 4:34). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-29.htm
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown call it a beautiful picture of piety, fidelity, and disinterestedness in a servant! https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_024.cfm

**vv. 34–35:** Guzik says Abraham's family may have wondered how he had done after leaving decades earlier. He notes the servant describes the blessing mainly in material terms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

**v. 36:** Utley thinks the mention of Sarah's old age was meant to reassure the family about Isaac's age. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-24
- Guzik says the point is that Isaac is the only heir to all of Abraham's wealth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

**vv. 37–38:** The Bible Hub study notes see the ban on a Canaanite wife as keeping the family's faith separate from pagan influence. https://biblehub.com/study/genesis/24-40.htm
- Other Bible Hub notes connect it with 2 Corinthians 6:14, the warning against being "unequally yoked." https://biblehub.com/genesis/24.htm
- Calvin, commenting earlier on vv. 2–4, says Abraham feared Isaac would "shake off the yoke of God" by marrying into peoples marked out for judgement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/genesis/24.htm

**v. 39:** Chuck Smith thinks the servant probably doubted he could persuade a young woman to come back with him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-40.html

**v. 40:** Matthew Henry says Abraham drew confidence from a clear conscience about how he had "walked before God," and links this to Genesis 17:1. Henry also notes the servant later worships God, not the angel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-40.html
- Poole explains "walk before" as obeying God's commands and trusting his promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-40.htm
- Henry adds that angels guide as well as protect the heirs of promise (Hebrews 1:14). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_024.cfm
- Guzik says Abraham never doubted God would lead the servant to the right woman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
- The nature of "His angel": see the differences section below.

**v. 41:** Guzik and Henry quote this verse (the release from the oath) but don't comment on it separately in what I read.

**vv. 42–44:** Matthew Henry says the servant's sign was a prayer, not an ultimatum. He warns against being over-bold in urging what God should do, in case the outcome weakens our faith instead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-27.htm
- Henry also says it is good dealing with those who by prayer take God along with them in their dealings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-40.html
- Maclaren (Baptist) calls the test homely. He stresses there was no miracle: God guided through ordinary, everyday acts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-27.htm
- *v. 43:* Utley notes Rebekah is called *bethulah* ("virgin") in v. 16 but *almah* ("maiden") here. The Septuagint translated *almah* as "virgin" both here and in Isaiah 7:14. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-24

**v. 45:** Coffman (on vv. 15–20) says God answered while the prayer was still on the servant's lips. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-20.html
- Guzik adds that the servant didn't yet *know* his prayer was answered; only time would show it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
- Bible Odyssey notes that young women usually drew the household's water. They most likely carried the jar on the shoulder, as Rebekah does. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/women-and-wells-in-the-hebrew-bible/

## Where commentators differ (not along denominational lines in what I found)

1. **Laban's motives (vv. 29–31):** Many read him as greedy. Henry imagines him thinking there is something to be got by, a man that is rich and generous. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_024.cfm
   - Coffman speaks of Laban's "cupidity" being aroused by the gifts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-20.html
   - The Pulpit Commentary takes the other side: it says Laban's character has been "considerably traduced" (unfairly blackened) and sees him as moved by generosity and hospitality. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-29.htm

2. **"I being in the way" (v. 27):** Maclaren admits the Hebrew can be read as simple emphasis ("As for me"). He still keeps the fuller sense: God guides those already walking the right path and doing the duty in front of them. He also adds a caution: We must wait till we are sure of God's will before we try to do it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-27.htm
   - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) uses the verse to urge believers to step out in faith; God leads one step at a time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-27.html

3. **Typology, i.e. reading the story as a picture of Christ:** Guzik reads it as the Father seeking a bride for the Son through a faithful servant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
   - Coffman quotes a writer who sees the unnamed servant as a picture of the Holy Spirit and Rebekah as the Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-1.html
   - Smith links Eliezer's name ("God my helper") to the Spirit as Helper. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-40.html
   - Deffinbaugh (bible.org) is more cautious: reading the chapter as a picture of the Trinity may be a good devotional thought but isn't the heart of the passage. https://bible.org/seriespage/25-how-find-godly-wife-genesis-241-67

4. **What "His angel" means (v. 40):** Barnes sees the Lord acting as a messenger without any visible appearance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/24-40.html
   - Bush (quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary) treats the angel as a personification of God's special providence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/genesis-24.html
   - A Bible Hub Q&A article insists angelic activity is "integral," not decoration. It says believers today may expect concrete guidance, including angelic help when God chooses. https://biblehub.com/q/Genesis_24_40_on_divine_intervention.htm
